extracted.intended_audience: general readers interested in humor, students of psychology/cognitive science, and comedians/joke-writers
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes psychological/cognitive theories and practical criteria for when a joke is perceived as funny, focusing on structure (setup/punchline), incongruity and its resolution, and norm-violation judged as benign. Useful for analyzing or writing jokes from a cognitive-humor perspective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Setup–punchline structure
rubrics_metrics.description: A joke is assumed to have a setup and a punchline; the structure matters for how humor unfolds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original wording: 'the structure of the joke is assumed to have a setup and a punchline.' The setup leads the audience to form predictions; the punchline subverts or shifts those predictions. Examples given include conventional joke forms used by stand-up comedians. Use a clear setup that creates expectations the punchline can meaningfully contradict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incongruity (bissociation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The punchline should be different from what you would predict from the setup; perceiving a disparity or 'bissociation' (two contradictory meanings) produces humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From Koestler's incongruity theory: 'the content of the joke must lead the audience to sense some disparity or incongruity between the setup and the punchline.' Examples: O’Riley armed-robbery 'Not guilty' → 'can I keep the money?' and Alingon Mitra's Instagram quote joke. Use incongruity that creates two competing interpretations; anti-pattern: no prediction/subversion so the incongruity is weak.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolution of incongruity ('getting the joke')
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor often depends not just on perceiving incongruity but on resolving it — reinterpreting the setup in light of the punchline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From Suls's incongruity-resolution theory: 'it is not the perception of incongruity but the resolution of incongruity, that is, ‘getting the joke’, that makes the joke funny.' The setup should be vague enough to allow reinterpretation when the punchline forces a new reading. Example: Abhishek Upmanyu popcorn-in-seat joke — resolution reinterprets 'not needing to buy popcorn' as a negative. Empirical support: Shultz & Horibe (1974) found original jokes with both incongruity+resolution produced more mirth than versions with only one component.

rubrics_metrics.name: Both incongruity and resolution contribute to funniness
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes that contain both an incongruity and a resolvable reinterpretation elicit more mirth than jokes with only one of these elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study cited: Shultz & Horibe (1974) presented three versions of a joke to children; mirth was highest for the original (both incongruity and resolution), intermediate for incongruity-only, and lowest for resolution-only. Use both elements when possible; if only one is present expect reduced funniness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benign violation (norm-violation + perceived harmlessness)
rubrics_metrics.description: A joke will be funny if it (1) violates some norm and (2) the violation is perceived as benign by the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From Warren & McGraw (2015): 'the joke should violate a norm, but the violation should be perceived as benign.' Norms may be social, moral, ethical, or linguistic. Examples: O’Riley violates self-preservation/justice norms but is benign because he is hypothetical; Alingon Mitra's scientific violation is benign because it has no real consequences; Abhishek Upmanyu's popcorn joke violates hygiene norms but is benign. Anti-pattern: a violation that is not perceived as benign (too severe) will not be funny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Window/degree of violation
rubrics_metrics.description: The norm-violation must fall within a narrow window: not so small that it isn't perceived as a violation, and not so big that it is non-benign/unacceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original wording: 'the violation should be within a small window, not too small as not to be considered a violation, and not too big to be considered non-benign/unacceptable.' Practical implication: calibrate how transgressive a joke is for the audience; pushing beyond the audience's benign threshold makes the joke offensive rather than funny. Example: changing the popcorn-to-medicine in a hospital makes the violation severe and non-benign.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type of norm and context sensitivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Which norm is violated (social, moral, ethical, linguistic) and the context determine whether the violation is perceived as benign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'norm' is broadly defined; context can flip a benign violation into a harmful one. Example: same punchline (dropped item on seat) is benign in a theater but would be non-benign if the item were medicine in a hospital. Guidance for writers: consider audience, setting, and which norm is at stake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relatability / observation-based comedy as benign violation
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation-based jokes can be funny when they present an unusual observation that violates an expectation but is relatable, thus perceived as a benign violation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The blog notes that benign violation theory can explain observation/relatable comedy: 'the “violation” of the norm can be viewed in terms of an unusual observation about a topic such that you never thought of it that way, but it is relatable.' Use surprising but recognizable insights about common experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasant incongruities that propagate norms tend not to be funny (dad-joke anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Incongruities that are 'pleasant' or that propagate a norm (i.e., do not violate it) are less likely to be perceived as funny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the dad-joke 'That would be a big step forward' is clever wordplay but does not violate a norm, which may explain why it is not very funny. The blog suggests such jokes may only be amusing due to meta-norm expectations (people laughing at 'lame' jokes). Avoid relying solely on punny wordplay without any norm-violation or meaningful incongruity-resolution if the goal is stronger laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vagueness in setup as a device to permit reinterpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: A setup should be sufficiently vague to allow the punchline to force a reinterpretation that resolves incongruity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From the incongruity-resolution discussion: 'the setup must also be vague enough to allow a reinterpretation when the incongruity is resolved.' Practical tip: craft setups that lead listeners to a plausible reading but leave alternative readings possible so the punchline can flip the frame.

rubrics_metrics.name: Awareness of multiple theories (comprehension–elaboration and others)
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple theories exist to explain humor (e.g., comprehension–elaboration as a variant of incongruity-resolution); different theories emphasize different mechanisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The blog notes other contemporary theories like comprehension–elaboration but does not elaborate. Practical implication: when analyzing or composing humor, consider multiple complementary mechanisms — motivation-based (superiority/relief), incongruity+resolution, benign violation, comprehension–elaboration — since different jokes may rely on different processes.
